attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: 'I think ... will' states a belief about a definite future outcome. It is not one of the probability hedges listed in the policy, so it is scored as a forecast. No horizon is given, and the proposition keeps both categories.

contract.note: The plain reading, that LLM use eventually concentrates in expensive local enthusiast setups and niche enterprise roles, is ordinary and fair. Because there is no deadline, only a durable, decisive deployment pattern can resolve it.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure (Nov 2025) of enterprise seat growth. It is a company statement about itself and shows interim adoption, not an eventual endpoint.
Preprint posted before the evaluation date. It shows broad enterprise use through March 2026, which is interim data and cannot settle an undated forecast about the eventual market.

reviews.rationale: This is a forecast with no deadline. The evidence shows broad interim enterprise and consumer use, which runs against the forecast so far. It does not establish a durable mature deployment pattern either way, and the early-resolution rule is not met. So the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: This is an observation about the share of AI capex plus an evaluative clause about systemic weakness. The majority threshold is kept.

contract.note: Defining big tech as the four companies he names in context, and using the Q2 2025 quarter, are reasonable readings. Treating systemic weakness as material US economic exposure is an ordinary plain reading.

evidence.note: IDC estimate as reported by The Next Platform: 86.7% of Q2 AI infrastructure spending came from a broader group of cloud providers. It covers servers and storage only, so it is a different group and different asset coverage than the four companies' share of all AI capex.
Fed note explaining that hyperscaler capex includes non-AI spending. It gives no share for the target quarter and does not quantify systemic exposure.

reviews.rationale: No comparable numerator and denominator isolate the four companies' AI capex in Q2 2025. The 86.7% figure covers a broader buyer group and narrower assets. No evidence quantifies the US systemic exposure. Neither component is settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the exception, 'doesn't seem', and the $9.9 billion valuation (Cursor). It is an impressionistic observation about acquisition demand at the time of publication.

contract.note: Three readings come from the evaluator, not the speaker: Cursor plus comparable firms as the scope, Cognigy as the exception, and the year-to-date period. They are reasonable, but the result depends on them. Requiring bids near the valuation is fair.

evidence.note: TechCrunch (Apr 2025) reports that OpenAI and others approached Anysphere. The prices are unspecified and the approaches came before the $9.9B valuation, so they do not meet the contract's standard.
Cursor's own disclosure of its $9.9B financing valuation. It identifies the company but says nothing about acquisition offers.

reviews.rationale: Acquisition interest in Cursor existed, but no reported offer is near $9.9B in the target period. Public reporting also cannot show that private interest was absent. The evidence neither establishes a lack of buyer appetite at that valuation nor shows a credible bid.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: This is a numerical observation about past cash burn. 'Appears' softens it but does not remove the at-least-$10B assertion for the two-month window.

contract.note: Reading 'burned' as net business cash consumption, excluding financing, is the ordinary meaning. The window of June 6 to August 6, 2025 follows his wording.

evidence.note: Reuters, citing The Information (unverified): $2.5B burned in H1 2025 and an $8.5B full-year target. These cover different periods and include a projection, so they are strong countercontext but not a measurement of the window.
CNBC sources (Feb 2026) report $8B of cash burn for all of 2025. That is far below the claimed two-month amount, but it is an annual figure without the breakdown for the window.

reviews.rationale: The reported H1 and full-year burn figures ($2.5B and $8B) make $10B in two months very implausible. Still, they cover different periods and come from unverified sourced reports. Under the rule, evidence about a different period is context only, and no cash-flow record covers the window, so the claim stays unresolved.
